memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then Jacob called for his sons and said: 'Gather around so I can tell you what will happen to you in days to come. Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to your father Israel.'" — Gen 49:1-2 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Twelve grown men gather around a dying father's bed. What follows is one of the longest prophetic passages in Genesis — a word over each son about what lies ahead for the tribes that will come from them.

Before a single word of blessing, Jacob says: listen.

That is not a small instruction. These are men in their forties, fifties and sixties, some of them wealthy, some of them powerful. They are long past the age of being told what to do. And they gather anyway, because their father has something to say and they know it is worth hearing.

There is a discipline here that we lose easily. Listening requires us to stop talking, stop planning our reply, and receive something we did not generate ourselves. It is the posture of a learner, and we do not naturally hold it — least of all as we grow older and more established.

Yet Scripture insists on it constantly. Everyone should be quick to listen and slow to speak (Jas 1:19). Jesus said repeatedly, "Whoever has ears, let them hear."

Before God speaks to us through His Word, the first question is not whether we agree. It is whether we are actually listening.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. When did you last genuinely listen rather than wait for your turn to speak?
2. Are you still teachable, or have you quietly stopped learning?
3. What might God be saying that you have not slowed down enough to hear?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, make me quick to listen and slow to speak. Give me a teachable heart before Your Word, however old or established I become. Amen.
